St. Romanus the Melodist

Saints

St. Romanus the Melodist

Period
Byzantine period; exact chronology not established here
Region
Constantinople
Titles / vocation
Hymnographer · Deacon
Commemoration
October 1

Introduction

St. Romanus is remembered as a deacon and hymnographer associated with Constantinople. The OCA account describes his early difficulties as a singer, a traditional vision of the Mother of God, and his later hymn composition. It places his death around 556. The vision is presented as a feature of the received life, while particular hymn texts require their own identified editions.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

GOARCH places Romanos in Emesa in Syria, probably in a Jewish family, and records Christian baptism and service as a deacon at Beirut. It links the Semitic idiom of his writings with that background. This biographical outline should be distinguished from the detailed story of his miraculous gift of song, transmitted in the later feast-day tradition.

[2] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section

Life and notable events

The OCA narrative places St. Romanus at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Humiliated by unsuccessful reading during Nativity services, he receives a vision of the Mother of God and a scroll, then sings the Nativity kontakion. This is the transmitted hagiographic account of his gift.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative and concluding account

Death and martyrdom

The OCA Life places his repose around 556 after continued hymn-writing. It reports neither execution nor a medical cause.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative and concluding account

Writings and legacy

Romanus (9), St., a celebrated hymn writer of the Eastern church, who is said to have written more than 1,000 hymns, of the kind called kontakia, a form which he probably invented. It perhaps derives its some what disputed name from the legend as to its origin, found in the Synaxasion of St. Romanus's day (Menaea, Oct. 1), which says that the Blessed Virgin appeared to him, and commanded him to eat a roll (kontakion) which she gave him, and that, obeying, he found himself endowed with the power of composing hymns. If he was the first who wrote kontakia, it is an argument in favour of placing him (as do Pitra and the Bollandists) in the reign of Anastasius I. (491-518) rather than of Anastasius II. (713-719). [H.A.W.]

[3] Historical Anglican biographical reference · Entry “Romanus(9)”; complete bounded biographical paragraph

GOARCH identifies the Nativity kontakion as a foremost example of his work and notes the influence of Ephraim’s hymns. The historical dictionary also distinguishes competing chronological placements, preferring the earlier Anastasius. Claims of a thousand compositions belong to the transmitted reputation; they should not imply that a thousand complete, securely attributed texts survive.

[2] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section · [3] Historical Anglican biographical reference · Romanus entry; competing chronological placements
